Yes, the quarterback is a rookie with no playoff experience, but if he's your franchise player for the future, you need to get him acclimated to a playoff atmosphere at some point, especially if you're planning on a multi-year championship window. Otherwise, you're just shooting yourself in the foot for the next time you make the playoffs!

I know there are no moral victories in football, but there is gain to be had beyond the previous season. Next time the quarterback leads the team to the playoffs, he'll be older, wiser, and more experienced. Call me crazy, but the moment the veteran quarterback went down, any thoughts of instant gratification became a fool's errand. The moment the veteran went down, I lost all faith that he could establish the team as a dominant force within the conference. The moment the veteran went down, the plan was survival, and nothing else.

But the rookie saved the team from the challenges that were the conference, teeming with the likes of other strong teams. The rookie didn't help you survive.

He helped you thrive.

He helped you conquer.

He helped you reach the safe haven that we call the NFL Postseason.

And though you ultimately didn't get to savor the fruits of victory, you became all the stronger for it, maybe strong enough to finally reach that promised land with the wisdom the rookie has gained all throughout this season. And that is why I will never take seriously anyone who says the veteran should have started over the rookie.

The sudden death rules were a set of regulations used in various sports to determine the winner of a tied game. Under these rules, the first team to score during an overtime period would immediately win the game, eliminating the need for a full additional period of play. This format was intended to create a more exciting and decisive conclusion to games, often leading to dramatic moments as teams fought to score first.
